title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 7)
summary: Part 7 of NH's reading of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations. He covers the traits that disqualify someone from Stoicism and the leader-group symbiosis, then the line about being neither tyrant nor slave. He also discusses mental slavery, the emptiness of fame, nature as endless change, facing death, studying other people, and evil as a perception you can refuse.
claims: Stoicism can exist in isolation but works best applied to society and community
Marcus believed everyone has reason; many people are stupid not by birth but because they choose not to use it
Leader and group are symbiotic: the group needs the leader, but without the group the leader's life loses meaning, so they are equal in value
Modern support systems keep unproductive people on crutches, so they never learn to walk on their own
The Stoic is neither tyrant nor slave: he refuses to be subjugated and refrains from subjugating, willing to lead but never to own
Owning or dominating others is still a burden, because it diverts energy from improving yourself
There are far more mental slaves than physical ones, possibly billions, and they put the chains on themselves and can remove them
Fame is empty: even the brightest fame fades, and it does nothing for the soul; focus on just actions, sincere speech and accepting what happens
Nature imposes endless change; whatever refuses to evolve disappears, and species like some sharks and spiders stayed unchanged only because nothing challenged them
Humans perceive natural events as personal challenges, which is both useful (we build lasting shelters) and harmful (victim mentality)
Once you accept and appreciate change as coming from the same source as you, anxiety, anger and difficulty disappear and you become flexible
Reframing difficulties as new tests turns life from a miserable experience into a game; you are on earth to have fun
The sweet spot about death lies between accepting it, being willing to meet it, and wanting to die: meet death head-on while not wanting to die
Every serious philosophy, including the Hagakure and the Book of Five Rings, deals with accepting death, and a new life begins once you do
Study other people: reading their thoughts and emotions raises emotional IQ and makes you more effective, whereas most treat others as NPCs
Watching the powerful shows they are not special; their power rests on your belief in it, and seeing others' vulnerability makes you less vulnerable
Evil lies in your perception of what hurts you; refusing that perception means you do not judge others as evil and are not hurt by words
Shared taboos across isolated cultures tend to protect society and its weaker members
Perceiving evil to protect the group is good; perceiving it only to protect yourself from words is what Marcus says to reject
The pinnacle of Stoicism would be staying calm inside while a thousand people verbally attack you; he admits he is not there yet
